newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: World solar summit seeks cash to back power plans.
newsitem.headline: World solar summit seeks cash to back power plans.

text.p: A world solar summit drew to a close on Tuesday with delegates seeking ways to raise cash to back political support for a plan aimed at providing energy to 2.4 billion people living without electricity around the globe.
In addresses to the two-day World Solar Summit, several delegates called on Western donors to help them turn their plans into reality, and the dark world into light.

"We appeal to the international community, to the United Nations and its specialised agencies and the developed countries in particular, to provide the developing world with financial and technical assistance," Chinese state counsellor Luo Gan said.

International Energy Agency executive director Robert Priddle said the Third World's answer to financial problems lay in opening itself to foreign investment to develop the required solar and other renewable energy sources.
"Major private sector investment will be essential (and) those with the vision to liberalise energy markets and open up to outside investment would create exciting opportunities," he said.
Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa backed Priddle's statement, but said there was also great need to mobilise domestic savings through sound economic management for this purpose.
Organisers said the World Solar Summit was due to adopt resolutions encompasing all these points later on Tuesday.

The summit -- which is being attended by delegates, including 12 heads of state and governments, from 100 countries -- was called up to drum up political support for the use of solar and other renewable sources of energy.

But during the conference, a number of leaders have shifted the focus to the need for concrete financial backing for a long- term United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organistion (UNESCO) programme to provide energy to all by the middle of the next century.
About 300 solar and other renewable sources of energy projects from 59 countries were presented to the summit and delegates were early on Tuesday discussing possible sources of finance for them.

On Monday, Pakistani President Farooq Ahmad Khan Leghari commended the World Bank for its recent pledge to help promote the use of solar and other renewable sources of energy, but said there was a disappointing lack of commitment from other donors.

"We hope that other multilateral agencies such as the Asian Development Bank, the Islamic Development Bank and also enlightened donor countries will commit themselves to the idea of the solar energy system and all such organisations will truly reflect this commitment through their programmes," he said.

When he opened the summit, Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe said funding for renewable energies averaged only three percent of multilateral banks' lending portfolios. He said this was ironic in view of the value of the emerging worldwide market for renewable energy technologies estimated at $40 billion a year.
The conference said the world should be convinced that solar, wind, geothermal and other renewable sources of energy were generally cheaper, environmentally friendly and easily accessible.
